title: The leper by the fire
hook: a man with leprosy scratches his sores by the fire and calls it pleasure

segments.voice: Yesterday: ditthi, and Sāriputta, fanning the Buddha, set free. Your line: noticing the grip of an opinion.

A mosquito bite on the ankle. Scratching it is a bad idea, it gets scratched anyway, and for a few seconds that feels like relief. Then it's worse. A wandering ascetic named Māgandiya hears that the Buddha teaches restraint of the senses, and he's offended. He calls the Buddha a destroyer of growth, someone who kills off life's pleasures. The Buddha doesn't get defensive. He tells Māgandiya about his own youth: three palaces, one for each season, musicians, pleasures on offer. He gave it all up. Why would anyone do that? He answers with a picture far stronger than a mosquito bite.
screen: `THE MOSQUITO BITE.` → `A DESTROYER OF GROWTH?` → `THREE PALACES, GIVEN UP.`

segments.voice: Suppose, the Buddha says, there were a man with leprosy, his body covered in sores. His only relief is to scratch the sores with his nails and hold his body over a pit of burning coals. The heat eases the itch. To him, it feels good. Now suppose a physician comes and cures him. He's healthy, free, able to go where he likes. Would he envy another sick man scratching by the fire? No. And if two strong men tried to drag him toward the coals, he'd twist and fight to get away. The coals are as hot as ever. What changed is his health. When he was sick, his senses were damaged, and so he took something painful to be pleasant. That's the Buddha's point about cravings, and it isn't puritan. He doesn't say pleasure is evil. He says some of what we call pleasure is relief from an itch the craving itself keeps making. The more you scratch, the more it itches. Then the Buddha speaks a verse: health is the greatest gain, nibbāna the highest happiness. Māgandiya says he has heard those very words from his own teachers. So what is this health? Māgandiya rubs his own arms and legs: this is health. The Buddha says he knows the words, but not yet what they point to. A similar verse appears in the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's words: "Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvâna the highest happiness." The healed man doesn't hate the fire. He just doesn't need it anymore.
screen: `SORES, AND A PIT OF COALS.` · `THE PHYSICIAN CURES HIM.` · `THE FIRE IS THE SAME. HE ISN'T.` · `HEALTH, THE GREATEST GIFT.` · then, large: `THE LEPER'S FIRE.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you reach for that brings relief more than joy, checking, snacking, refreshing, rereading an old argument, and picture the moment just before you reach. Feel the itch there, the restlessness, and breathe into it without scratching. Notice that it rises and, if you wait, begins to fade.
Sukha. A sick man finds relief in burning coals and calls it pleasure; once healed, he wouldn't go near them.
Your line: the leper's fire. Relief from an itch isn't the same as ease. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use this simile to explain why monastics and serious lay practitioners restrain the senses: not because pleasure is evil, but because craving feeds itself, and a calm mind finds deeper ease.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit sukha: ease, happiness, pleasure. the sutta asks what real sukha is.

trapdoor: what you thought: the leper enjoys the fire.
what it means: what feels pleasant to the sick may be painful to the healthy; craving makes relief look like joy.
what a scholar hears: MN 75, the Māgandiya Sutta, at Kammāsadhamma in the Kuru country; the verse 'health is the greatest gain, nibbāna the highest bliss' is echoed in Dhammapada 204.

chat.says: Is Buddhism against enjoying life? It sounds like giving up every pleasure.
options: The Buddha said some pleasure is just relief from an itch that craving keeps making.
Yes: in this sutta the Buddha tells Māgandiya that all pleasure is evil.
No: the Buddha told Māgandiya to go back to his three palaces.
chat.meaning: In MN 75 the healed man won't go near the coals that once felt good. Craving makes relief from an itch look like joy.

Māgandiya.meaning: a wandering ascetic who called the Buddha a destroyer of growth

nibbāna.meaning: the freedom the Buddha taught; the verse calls it the highest happiness

Dhammapada.meaning: a well-loved collection of the Buddha's short verses

notes: MN 75 paraphrased; check the leper simile (scratching sores, cauterizing over a charcoal pit; healed man dragged by two strong men) and the three palaces.
Dhammapada 204 quoted from memory in Müller's wording; please confirm against SBE 10.
The leprosy image is ancient; the script frames it as 'in that ancient world, with no cure' and uses 'a man with leprosy'. The index title keeps 'leper'; a Keeper or the owner may prefer to retitle.
Māgandiya's word bhūnahu is rendered 'destroyer of growth'; confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): Māgandiya in MN 75 is a wanderer (paribbājaka), not a brahmin (the brahmin Māgandiya is Sn 4.9); corrected. The verse 'ārogyaparamā lābhā...' is spoken by the Buddha, and Māgandiya says he heard it from earlier teachers and then points to his own body as 'health'; the old order (Māgandiya quoting it) was reversed and is fixed. Removed 'in that ancient world, with no cure', which contradicted the simile's physician who cures him. Hook no longer tells the listener what they do; 'Imagine' changed to the sutta's 'Suppose'.
